related_questions.question: What is the most common radiation therapy?
related_questions.snippet: The most common kind is external beam radiation therapy. This treatment uses a large machine called a linear accelerator. High-energy beams are aimed from the machine to a precise point on your body. Radiation treatment that goes inside the body is called brachytherapy (brak-e-THER-uh-pee).

related_questions.question: What is the safest radiation therapy?
related_questions.snippet: Proton therapy generates virtually no exit dose. While the treatment effects of photon and proton radiation may be similar, the precision of proton therapy often makes it a safer choice with fewer aftereffects for certain types of tumors.

related_questions.question: What is the new type of radiation therapy?

text_blocks.snippet: Several new and advanced radiation therapy techniques are emerging, offering more precise and effective cancer treatment with fewer side effects compared to traditional methods. Proton therapy, stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), and image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) are among the latest advancements. Flash therapy, while still in early stages, shows promise in minimizing damage to healthy tissue.
snippet_highlighted_words: Proton therapy, stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), and image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT)

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of some key advancements:

list.title: Precision:
list.snippet: Proton therapy uses protons instead of X-rays, allowing for more targeted radiation delivery to the tumor.

list.title: Reduced Side Effects:
list.snippet: The ability to precisely target tumors minimizes damage to surrounding healthy tissue, potentially leading to fewer side effects.

list.title: Suitable for Certain Cancers:
list.snippet: Proton therapy is particularly useful for cancers near critical organs like the brain or heart.

list.title: May be used as a sole treatment or with other therapies
High Doses, Fewer Sessions:
list.snippet: SBRT delivers high doses of radiation in a smaller number of treatment sessions compared to traditional radiation therapy.

list.title: Precise Targeting:
list.snippet: SBRT uses advanced imaging and delivery techniques to target tumors with extreme accuracy, minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue.

list.title: Lung Tumors and Other Areas:
list.snippet: SBRT is commonly used for lung tumors and other cancers in areas where precision is crucial.

list.title: Real-time Monitoring:
list.snippet: IGRT combines X-ray imaging with radiation therapy, allowing doctors to track changes in tumor location and shape during treatment.

list.title: Adaptive Treatment:
list.snippet: This real-time monitoring enables adjustments to the radiation beam, ensuring accurate targeting even if the tumor shifts.

list.title: Minimizing Healthy Tissue Exposure:
list.snippet: IGRT helps minimize radiation exposure to healthy tissues by allowing for daily adjustments to the treatment plan.

list.title: Ultra-Fast Delivery:
list.snippet: Flash therapy delivers radiation at extremely high speeds (in milliseconds).

list.title: Potential for Reduced Side Effects:
list.snippet: Early research suggests that flash therapy may cause less damage to normal cells compared to conventional radiation.

list.title: In Early Stages:
list.snippet: Flash therapy is still under investigation and clinical trials are ongoing.

text_blocks.snippet: Radiation therapy, used to treat cancer and other conditions, can be broadly categorized into two main types: external beam radiation therapy and internal radiation therapy. External beam radiation therapy delivers radiation from a machine outside the body, while internal radiation therapy involves placing radioactive material inside the body.
snippet_highlighted_words: external beam radiation therapy and internal radiation therapy

list.title: 3D Conformal Radiation Therapy (3D-CRT):
list.snippet: Uses 3D images to precisely target the tumor, aiming radiation from multiple angles.

list.title: Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT):
list.snippet: Delivers varying intensities of radiation to the tumor, minimizing exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

list.title: Image-Guided Radiation Therapy (IGRT):
list.snippet: Uses imaging during treatment to precisely target the radiation, often with daily scans.

list.title: Stereotactic Radiosurgery (SRS) / Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT):
list.snippet: Delivers high doses of radiation to a very specific area, often in a single session (SRS) or a few sessions (SBRT).

list.title: Proton Therapy:
list.snippet: Uses protons instead of X-rays to target tumors, potentially minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue.

list.title: Total Body Irradiation (TBI):
list.snippet: A type of EBRT that irradiates the entire body, often in preparation for stem cell transplant.

list.title: Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT):
list.snippet: A form of IMRT that uses a rotating arc to deliver radiation, allowing for faster treatment times.

list.title: Surface Guided Radiation Therapy (SGRT):
list.snippet: Uses cameras to track a patient's skin surface during treatment, enhancing precision and potentially eliminating the need for skin tattoos.

list.title: MRI-guided Radiation Therapy:
list.snippet: Combines MRI with a linear accelerator to provide real-time imaging during treatment, allowing for adjustments based on tumor movement or changes.

list.title: Interstitial Brachytherapy:
list.snippet: Radioactive sources are placed directly into the tumor tissue.

list.title: Intracavitary Brachytherapy:
list.snippet: Radioactive sources are placed into a body cavity, like the uterus or vagina.

list.title: Intraluminal Radiation Therapy:
list.snippet: Radioactive sources are placed within a hollow organ, like the esophagus or trachea.

list.title: Systemic Radiation Therapy:
list.snippet: Radioactive material is administered intravenously or orally, targeting cancer cells throughout the body.
